Microwave assisted alkaline deep eutectic solvents treatment inducing deconstruction of recalcitrant moso bamboo cell walls for highly efficient dual-enzymatic saccharification
Junpeng Liu ⁿ, Ying Xie ⁿ, Xuan Xu ⁿ, Rongrong Xiang ⁿ, Chengyu Zhang ⁿ, Zhe Ji⁻, Qiang Yong ⁿ, Zhe Lingⁿ,*

ª Jiangsu Co-Innovation Center of Efficient Processing and Utilization of Forest Resources, College of Chemical Engineering, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, China ᵇ College of Marine Science and Bioengineering, Qingdao University of Science and Technology, Qingdao 266042, China
ARTICLE INFO --- **Keywords:** Biomass conversion Alkaline deep eutectic solvent Lignocellulose fractionation Enzymatic hydrolysis Moso bamboo

ABSTRACT Green and efficient deconstruction and valorization of lignocellulosic biomass remain as a hot topic for biorefinery research. Herein, novel alkaline arginine-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) pretreatment was employed to achieve efficient fractionation of highly recalcitrant moso bamboo. Higher solvent basicity was revealed for the proposed DESs with Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters values of α (0.292), β (0.845), and π* (1.284). Thus, a high (β-α) value was achieved, favorable for forming stronger hydrogen bonds with lignin and xylan for subsequent separation. Supramolecular structural changes of DESs-treated bamboo cellulose were quantitatively calculated, suggesting increased crystallinity index and decreased crystallite size that were beneficial for the following enzymatic degradation. The DESs pretreatment dramatically increased the removal rate of lignin (as high as 94.4%) and xylan (75.6%), greatly enhancing subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis with the highest saccharification yield rate of 91.8%, 9.8 folds as compared to that of raw bamboo biomass. Critical factors affecting enzymatic conversion performance of the bamboo cellulose were integrated, showing strong correlations with xylan removal (R² = 0.91), lignin removal (R² = 0.99), and cellulose crystallite size reduction (R² = 0.852). Mass balance of the present bioconversion process was performed. Based on a 100 g bamboo material balance, 51.97 g of high output fermentable sugars (including 43.96 g of glucose and 7.83 g of xylose) can be obtained after a 15-minute short pretreatment at 130 °C. Therefore, the proposed arginine-based alkaline DESs pretreatment offers new insights into the enhanced processing and bioconversion of lignocellulosic biomass.

1. Introduction Due to overconsumption of fossil resources and serious environ- mental pollution, exploration for environmentally friendly and renew- able alternatives has received more and more attention [1]. In recent decades, biorefining of lignocellulosic biomass has been considered as an ideal approach [2,3]. However, the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic biomass, such as moso bamboo, induced by the factors of lignin content, cell wall thickness, cellulose crystallinity, polymer orientation, lignin- carbohydrate complex (LCC) linkages, hemicellulose branching, and intricate anatomical structures etc., has consistently posed a significant barrier to the efficient conversion of biomass into renewable energy and

chemicals [4,5]. Therefore, exploring fascinating solvents for effective pretreatment and deconstruction of recalcitrant lignocellulose cell walls, as well as separating the major components for further bioconversion remain a hot topic but not well addressed.

Among the reported lignocellulosic pretreatment approaches, ionic liquids (ILs) have emerged as promising solvents for biomass pretreat- ment due to their wide liquid range, high solvating ability, and high ionic conductivity [6]. While, growing environmental and economic concerns limit their industrial applications [7]. With the introduction and development of green chemistry, the adoption of low- environmental impact processing technologies for producing high- value-added products from lignocellulosic raw materials has become a

highly challenging task [8–10]. Recently, DESs have stood out in green biocatalysis and biotransformation with the advantages of low cost, simple synthesis, and environmental sustainability. DESs are consist of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), usually using quaternary ammonium salts as HBAs, and acids, bases, carbohydrates, and phenolic substances as HBDs [11,12]. Therefore, DESs consisting different molar ratios of HBAs and HBDs may have many possible combinations, affecting their physical and chemical properties [13]. In recent years, numerous studies have been carried out using acidic DESs, such as Brønsted acidic DESs (BADESs) or Lewis acidic DESs (LADESs) for the fractionation and valorization of biomass [14]. In Lewis acidic DESs, these compounds with Lewis acidity are usually combined with other compounds (e.g., urea, ethylene glycol, etc.) to form eutectic mixtures through hydrogen bonding [15,16]. For example, the introduction of Lewis acids (AlCl3, FeCl3, FeCl2, ZnCl2 and CuCl2) into choline chloride/glycerol to make a ternary DES for the efficient pretreatment of hybrid beteljack energy grasses produces high purity and oxidative-resistant lignin [17]. In Brønsted acidic DESs, these acidic compounds usually combine with hydrogen bonding acceptors (e.g., quaternary ammonium salts, alcohols, etc.) to form eutectic mixtures with low melting points and high stability [18]. For example, DESs combined with choline chloride (ChCl) and natural p-coumaric acid (PCA) was applied for pretreatment on switchgrass under 160 °C, which induced 70 % of xylan removal [19]. However, acidic DESs will provide protons to catalyze the random cleavage of glycosidic bonds in xylan, leading to its hydrolysis to xylose, which was possibly dehydrated to furfural catalyzed by Brønsted and Lewis acids [20]. These degradation products will inhibit downstream hydrolysis and fermentation, which must be achieved after the detoxification process continued efficient biotransformation [21]. Therefore, in order to maximize product revenues from lignocellulosic, it is important to adopt efficient DESs to deal with the challenges of acidic conditions. Compared to neutral or acidic environments, polysaccharides showed less degradation under mild alkaline DESs conditions, which also effectively reduce the formation of inhibitors [22]. Meanwhile, the recovered hemicellulose has a higher molecular weight, thus adding additional high economic value to the production process [23]. It is also deserved to note that, lignin condensation also occurs in the intense acid treatment, hindering further bioconversion of the treated lignocellulose. Comparatively, alkali treatment process usually does not require high temperatures and also reduces the occurrence of condensation reactions [24,25]. For example, alkaline DESs (choline chloride/glycol/Na2S) incorporated by Na2S greatly facilitated the decomposition of lignin with a removal rate of up to 74.67%, while maximizing the retention of glucan and hemicellulose [26]. Thus, it is crucial and emerging to find suitable alkaline DESs to achieve efficient biotransformation.

Among the chemicals consisting of alkaline DESs, choline hydroxide (ChOH) is an aqueous, low-cost, biodegradable basic ionic liquid, which can act as effictive HBA and provide an alkaline environment for DESs [27]. For example, choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) DESs with 11 wt % water were used to dissolve at least 9.5 wt% cellulose with the degree of polymerization (DP) of 926 within 30 min [10]. Pan and colleagues applied two choline hydroxide based DESs (choline hydroxide-glycerol and choline hydroxide-urea) pretreatment on wheat straw. It removed 73.9% and 75.6% of lignin respectively, which showed a better coupling effect than choline chloride acid DESs [28]. These literatures indicate that, ChOH-based DESs have great potential for pretreatment of biomass. Besides, natural origin of the components gives DESs a great edge over DESs because they are clearly less toxic and more environ- mentally friendly. Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESS) include amino acid-glycosyl DESs, amino acid-organic acid-DESs, and glycosyl DESs etc. [29-31]. Recently, our group reported a novel arginine/ lactic acid DES (1:7) pretreatment strategy on moso bamboo, reaching high lignin removal rate of 84.4% and the highest enzymatic conversion yield of 81.9% glucose [32]. Pretreatment on corncob by DESs con- sisting of amino acids (lysine, arginine, histidine) and betaine for 5 h at

60 °C, about 50% of xylan and 60% of lignin could be removed, as well as obtaining enzymatic hydrolysis yield of 60.8% [33]. These results demonstrated satisfactory lignin and hemicellulose extraction, along with a high hydrolysis rate, using NADESs pretreatments. The remarkable bioconversion performance makes NADESS well suited for the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. However, up till now, there are very limited reports on ChOH as a prerequisite for NADESS with the cooperation of bio-derived amino acid. Moreover, the attempt to apply ChOH-based NADESs on biomass treatment and the inner mechanisms on lignocellulose deconstruction have been rarely discussed.

In this study, natural choline hydroxide/arginine (CA) DESs were developed for the first time to pretreat highly recalcitrant moso bamboo with the assistance of microwave radiation in short treatment time. The polarity and viscosity of DESs with different molar ratios were studied and their pretreatment properties were characterized. The effect of DESs on the cell wall structure of bamboo was described through scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and laser confocal technology. X-ray diffraction was used to study the variations of aggregated and crystalline cellulose under the treatment of DESs and characterization of extracted lignin by 2D HSQC NMR spectroscopy. The correlation between lignin removal, xylan removal, crystal size of cellulose, and enzymatic hy- drolysis yield was analyzed to explore the influencing factors of enzy- matic hydrolysis. The DESs pretreatment strategy of bamboo was evaluated by material balance accounting. The present study proposing physicochemical properties and pretreatment effects of DESs may pro- vide a reliable basis for further application of biorefinery on lignocel- lulosic biomass by alkaline NADESs.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and chemicals Moso bamboo culms were provided by Yunnan Forestry Center. Bamboo powder (40–80 mesh) was extracted by soxhlet extraction (acetone–ethanol volume ratio 2:1) for 6 h to remove pigments and alcohols. Bamboo strips were cut into 10 µm-sized transverse and radial sections using a slicer (HM 325, Thermo Scientific, USA) and observed under microscope. L-arginine and choline hydroxide were obtained from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All other chemicals were purchased from Shanghai Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China) and used as received.

2.2. DES preparation and characterization Choline hydroxide solution was slowly dripped into arginine solution at a molar ratio of 1:1/ 2:1 with homogeneous stirring for 24 h. The mixture was rotary evaporated under negative pressure at 50 °C to remove water and dried under vacuum at 70 °C for 48 h. The prepared DESs were left overnight to observe their stability. The DES with molar ratios of 1:1 and 1:2 (arginine to choline) are labeled as CA1 and CA2, respectively, as shown in Table S1. The α, β, and π* of the prepared DESs were determined using N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (NEt2), 4-nitroaniline (NH2), and Nile red (NR) as dye indicators of solvent properties [34]. The maximum absorption wavelength λmax of the dye-DES mixture was determined between 350–700 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer and measured three times to minimize experimental errors. The parameters were calculated according to the following equation [35].

2.3. DES pretreatment Moso bamboo powder was mixed with DES at a solid-liquid ratio of 1:20 and added to PTFE microwave reactor. The mixture was heated at 600 W for 10 min and kept for 5 min using MDS-8G microwave disin- tegrator (SINEO, Shanghai, China). The microwave temperatures were set to 90 °C, 100 °C, 110 °C, 120 °C and 130 °C, respectively. At the end of the reaction, the solid residue was washed with 50% acetone solution and 1% NaOH aqueous solution, and then the solid residue was washed repeatedly with deionized water for neutrality. Part of the neutral ma- terial will be air-dried for subsequent testing and part will be placed at 4 °C for cellulase hydrolysis. The pretreated samples were named ac- cording to the type of DES and the pretreatment temperature, e.g., CA1 bamboo chips pretreated at 90 °C supplemented with microwave were called CA1-90, and the other samples were followed similarly.

The slices were fixed with nickel mesh and pretreated in DES at 90 °C for 4 h. The slices were washed with 50 % acetone solution, 1 % NaOH solution, and deionized water until neutral, then air-dried and used for subsequent microscopic examination. The CA1- and CA2-treated moso bamboo sections were respectively named CA1-90-S and CA2-90-S, as shown in Table S1.

The 20 mL sample suspension with a concentration of 5 % was prepared in a 50 mL conical flask using 0.1 M citrate buffer, 60 µL of tetracycline, and 20 FPU/g dextran cellulase. The reaction system was subjected to enzymatic hydrolysis in a water bath at 50 °C for 72 h. The supernatant was periodically taken to inactivate and centrifuged. The monosaccharides in the supernatant were analyzed by Shimadzu high-performance liquid chromatography. ### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. DES characterization The viscosity and Kamlet-Taft lysochromic parameters of two different molar ratios of DESs were characterized, and the results are listed in Table 1. Viscosity is an important parameter for DESs as solvents. The viscosities of CA1 and CA2 viscosity at room temperature, are 1026.3 mPa·s and 983.6 mPa·s, respectively. The values were far lower than the other arginine DESs, and even lower than the water content of 6.5 % wt of choline chloride-lactic acid classic system [37,38]. The low viscosity is conducive to the contact between DESs and bamboo feedstock, which may deconstructs lignocellulose through macromolecular mobility in shorter time [39].

The chemical properties of the proposed DESs are reflected by Kamlet-Taft solvent chromism parameters, which include α (hydrogen-bond acidity), β (hydrogen-bond basicity), and π* (polarity/polariz-ability) values [35]. DES with a larger (β-α) (net alkalinity) value is beneficial for dissolving lignin, while the solubility of xylan is linearly related to the β value [40]. As inferred from Table 1, the π* parameters are 1.270 (CA1) and 1.284 (CA2) respectively, which shows their high polarity and ability to construct non-specific interactions such as dipo-le-dipole interactions [41]. Meanwhile, CA1 and CA2 exhibit high (β-α) values, indicating their superior lignin removal performance when treating moso bamboo [42]. Higher β values of choline-arginine-based DES suggest a stronger hydrogen bond donor capacity of the DES. Be-sides, DES with high (β-α) values can form stronger hydrogen bonds with lignin and xylan, facilitating breakage of their non-covalent linkages with cellulose. Therefore, DES with higher β values and (β-α) values are more effective in the pretreatment of moso bamboo biomass [41].

3.2. Chemical compositional analysis The cellulose recovery and chemical composition of raw and pre-treated moso bamboo samples are listed in Fig. 1. The cellulose recovery of bamboo after CA1 pretreatment was generally above 90 %, but it decreased to 86.4 % after CA2 pretreatment. It has been reported that, high lignin removal rates are commonly accompanied by certain amount of sugars loss, which is attributed to the degradation of moso bamboo cellulose under highly alkaline solvents [43]. For example, acidic ChCl/ethylene glycol (EG) DESs were developed and with the optimizing of alkali dosage, the cellulose recovery decreased from 87.43 % to 79.91 % [44]. Therefore, it can be concluded that the lower the β values and (β-α) values, the more favorable the recovery of cellulose after DESs treatment.

When the temperature elevated from 90 °C to 130 °C, the increase of cellulose content and the decrease of lignin and xylan content were also observed, reaching 94.4% of lignin and 75.6% of xylan respectively (Fig. 1c and d). The lignin removal rate was significantly improved as compared to ChCl-EG/sodium sulfide DESs treatment by traditional heating method, which removed 56.85–74.67% lignin [26]. Hence, increasing pretreatment temperature significantly enhanced the removal of lignin and xylan [23]. It was therefore critical to increase the

In addition to pretreatment temperature, previous studies have also shown that pretreatment duration affects lignin removal. Hu et al. suggested that, EG/citric acid (CA) DES remove 47.07 %–51.48 % lignin from bamboo at 90 °C for 4 h–24 h by traditional heating method [45]. The conventional DES system composed of choline chloride/lactic acid (LA) only achieved a lignin removal rate of 84.1 % when treated at the same temperature for 90 min using traditional heating methods [46]. At the same temperature, the microwave-assisted arginine/choline DES pretreatment in this study required only 15 min to obtain a satisfying pretreatment effect. Compared with other arginine-based DESs and amino acid-based DESs, choline-arginine DESs in the present work show evidently better ability to remove lignin and xylan [47,48]. Meanwhile, the application of microwave-assisted pretreatment would make it easier for solvent molecules to penetrate the dense structure of bamboo and contact the binding site more easily, and thus showed stronger lignin and xylan removal ability [49].

3.3. Enzymatic hydrolysis The enzymatic hydrolysis yield is considered as an important index to evaluate the pretreatment effect of DESs. As shown in Fig. 2, direct cellulase hydrolysis of the original sample for 72 h resulted in a rather low glucose yield of 6.2%, which is consistent with previous research [50] (Fig. 2a). After pretreatment by CA1 and CA2, the glucose yield of bamboo increased to 69.5%–91.8% and 72.0%–86.0% (Fig. 2b and c), respectively. The glucose yields were 11.2–14.8 and 11.6–13.9 times higher than those of the original samples, respectively. It was higher than the conversion of samples pretreated with guanidine hydrochloride (GH)/urea (U) (90.79 wt%), GH/glycerol (Gly) (86.67 wt%), choline chloride/lactic acid (LA) (72.56 wt%), and GH/LA (50.09 wt%) DESs at 130 °C for 30 min [51]. The removal of lignin-carbohydrate complex by the DESs may be one of the major factors for improving the accessibility of enzymes to cellulose chains. Microwave-assisted CA1 reaction at 130 °C for 15 min can increase the glucose yield to 91.8%, and CA2 reaction at 90 °C can increase the conversion rate to 86.0%. The phenomena suggested the ideal pretreatment efficiency by choline-arginine DES properties.

With respect to conversion of hemicelluloses, the yield of xylose increased from 8.9% to 56.8%–71.4% for CA1 and 8.9% to 68.0%–76.8% for CA2 (Fig. 2d, e and f). The results showed that the pre-treatment performance of CA1 and CA2 was better than that of most alkaline DESs pretreatments, such as ChCl/guaiacol and ChCl/mono-ethanolamine DESs [52,53]. It has been reported that, alkaline DESs showed the capability to saponify and split the ester bonds between hemicellulose and other components [50]. In addition to the removal of acetyl groups and the weakening of hydrogen bonds between cellulose and hemicellulose, satisfying enzymatic degradability on both cellulose and hemicelluloses saccharides were achieved [54].

In order to furtherly show the relationship between the lignin and xylan removal rate by DESs and glucose yields by enzymatic hydrolysis, linear fitting plot was performed. As shown in Fig. S1, there was a high linear positive correlation between the removal rate of xylan and lignin of CA1 and its glucose yield, with R2 = 0.91 and 0.99. However, CA2 removal rate was negatively correlated with glucose yield. This is related to the structural changes caused by the removal of the outer envelope structure of cellulose in a highly alkaline environment [55].

### 3.5. Crystal structural analysis The effect of choline-arginine DESs on the crystal structure of bamboo cellulose was analysed by XRD. The XRD spectra of the raw and DESs-treated samples showed similar characteristic peaks (Fig. 5a), with four diffraction peaks at 2θ = 14.9°, 16.7°, 22.2° and 34.8°, which corresponded to (1 –1 0), (1 1 0), (2 0 0) and (0 0 4) surfaces,

respectively [60]. The present diffraction peaks are consistent with the standard characteristic peaks of natural cellulose Iß, indicating that the proposed choline-arginine DESs well maintained the initial crystalline allomorphs of bamboo cellulose.

The crystallinity, crystallite size and d-Spacing of the sample ob- tained after fitting are shown in Fig. 5b and c. The crystallinity of the untreated bamboo sample is about 73.1%, which increased to 73.5%- 79.5% after CA1 treatment. The increase of crystallinity was majorly caused by the successful removal of amorphous lignin and hemi- celluloses by the DESs. Overall, the crystallinity increases with increasing temperature and decreases slightly as the temperature is further increased above 120 °C due to disintegration of the cellulose crystalline zone. ### 3.6. Lignin characteristics 2D-HSQC NMR spectroscopy was used to investigate the chemical structural variations of lignin after DESs pretreatment. The two-dimensional map information of aliphatic region and aromatic region is shown in Fig. 7 and annotated according to previous literature [66]. Typical bonds of lignin were present in all samples, including β-O-4 bond structure (A), β-β bond structure (B), and β-5 bond structure (C).

Moreover, The observation of γ-acetylated β-O-4 bond (A') signals in pristine lignin samples represents the acetylation of the γ-C site of lignin and the appearance of acylated p-coumaric acid structure [8]. However, the signal was weakened under CA2 treatment at 90 °C and disappeared after CA1 treatment at 130 °C, indicating that the acetyl group was shed under alkaline DESs pretreatment and eliminated at high temperature [67]. At the same time, Aα, Aβ (S), and Aβ (G) correspond to Cα-Hα, Cβ-Hβ in β-O-4 bond of eugenic-based lignin and Cβ-Hβ in β-O-4 bond of guaiac-based lignin, respectively. After DESs treatment, the β-O-4 signal of lignin tends to decrease. It suggests that, alkaline DESs selectively cleaved a large number of β-O-4 ether bonds [4]. In addition to the cleavage of the β-O-4 bond, the contents of retinol β-β structure (B) and phenyl coumarin β-5 structure (C) were also reduced, suggesting that some C-C bonds were also degraded by choline-arginine DESs [68].

The main aromatic unit structure of phyllostachy lignin also appeared in Fig. 7, including syringyl (S), guaiacyl (G), and p-hydroxyphenyl (H). The S/G values of raw bamboo lignin, CA1 and CA2 pretreatment solution lignin were 1.1, 1.4 and 1.9, respectively, which were similar to the S/G results in other studies [69]. G lignin was reported to adsorb cellulase more readily than S lignin and H lignin. Therefore, the enzymatic efficiency of the samples containing more G lignin was lower than that of the samples containing less G lignin and the same trend was observed for moso bamboo [70,71]. Meanwhile, p-coumaric acid (PCA) and ferulic acid (FA) were abundant in the CA2 pretreatment solution, and the obvious signals were located at (PCA2,6), (PCA3,5), (PCAβ), and (FA2), respectively. Besides, the α signals of p-coumaric acid and ferulic acid overlapped at δC/δH144.6/7.5 ppm. It was seen that, FA and PCA are cleaved after treatment with the alkaline deep eutectic solvent CA2, preventing the formation of ester or ether bonds between the lignin and hemicelluloses. Therefore, the recalcitrance of the substrates caused by lignin-carbohydrate complex was proved to be cleaved by the proposed treatments, which enhanced the contact between substrates and cellulase enzymes [72].

## 4. Conclusion This study developed a rapid microwave-assisted choline-arginine deep eutectic solvent (DES) pretreatment to optimize the fractionation and enzymatic conversion of moso bamboo lignocellulose, revealing its high potential for selective delignification, carbohydrate recovery, and fermentable sugar production. Its high β value (0.845) and (β-α) value (0.554) demonstrate high selectivity for delignification, excellent carbohydrate recovery, and desirable fermentable sugar yields. Under optimal conditions (130 °C, 15 min, arginine:ChOH = 1:1, 20 FPU/g), it achieved a high delignification rate (94.4%) and xylan removal rate (75.6%), resulting in enhanced dual monosaccharide yields, with 91.8 % glucose yield and 71.4% xylose yield. Moreover, in the alkaline environment, the degradation of polysaccharides was greatly minimized, and the cleavage of alkali-unstable FA and PCA by choline-arginine DESs was observed, which were considered favorable factors for improving enzymatic hydrolysis yields. Pretreatment conditions under selected microwave-assisted methods were more effective in both improving results and reducing energy consumption compared to conventional heating conditions. Overall, the proposed arginine/ChOH DESs pretreatment strategy proved to be a low-cost and effective method, showing great application potential for lignocellulose deconstruction and conversion into bio-based chemicals.

Herein, novel alkaline arginine-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) pretreatment was employed to achieve efficient fractionation of highly recalcitrant moso bamboo. Higher solvent basicity was revealed for the proposed DESs with Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters values of α (0.292), β (0.845), and π* (1.284). Thus, a high (β-α) value was achieved, favorable for forming stronger hydrogen bonds with lignin and xylan for subsequent separation. Supramolecular structural changes of DESs-treated bamboo cellulose were quantitatively calculated, suggesting increased crystallinity index and decreased crystallite size that were beneficial for the following enzymatic degradation. The DESs pretreatment dramatically increased the removal rate of lignin (as high as 94.4%) and xylan (75.6%), greatly enhancing subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis with the highest saccharification yield rate of 91.8%, 9.8 folds as compared to that of raw bamboo biomass. Critical factors affecting enzymatic conversion performance of the bamboo cellulose were integrated, showing strong correlations with xylan removal (R² = 0.91), lignin removal (R² = 0.99), and cellulose crystallite size reduction (R² = 0.852). Mass balance of the present bioconversion process was performed. Based on a 100 g bamboo material balance, 51.97 g of high output fermentable sugars (including 43.96 g of glucose and 7.83 g of xylose) can be obtained after a 15-minute short pretreatment at 130 °C. Therefore, the proposed arginine-based alkaline DESs pretreatment offers new insights into the enhanced processing and bioconversion of lignocellulosic biomass. 1. Introduction Due to overconsumption of fossil resources and serious environ- mental pollution, exploration for environmentally friendly and renew- able alternatives has received more and more attention [1]. In recent decades, biorefining of lignocellulosic biomass has been considered as an ideal approach [2,3]. However, the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic biomass, such as moso bamboo, induced by the factors of lignin content, cell wall thickness, cellulose crystallinity, polymer orientation, lignin- carbohydrate complex (LCC) linkages, hemicellulose branching, and intricate anatomical structures etc., has consistently posed a significant barrier to the efficient conversion of biomass into renewable energy and chemicals [4,5]. Therefore, exploring fascinating solvents for effective pretreatment and deconstruction of recalcitrant lignocellulose cell walls, as well as separating the major components for further bioconversion remain a hot topic but not well addressed. Among the reported lignocellulosic pretreatment approaches, ionic liquids (ILs) have emerged as promising solvents for biomass pretreat- ment due to their wide liquid range, high solvating ability, and high ionic conductivity [6]. While, growing environmental and economic concerns limit their industrial applications [7]. With the introduction and development of green chemistry, the adoption of low- environmental impact processing technologies for producing high- value-added products from lignocellulosic raw materials has become a * Corresponding author. Recently, DESs have stood out in green biocatalysis and biotransformation with the advantages of low cost, simple synthesis, and environmental sustainability. DESs are consist of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), usually using quaternary ammonium salts as HBAs, and acids, bases, carbohydrates, and phenolic substances as HBDs [11,12]. Therefore, DESs consisting different molar ratios of HBAs and HBDs may have many possible combinations, affecting their physical and chemical properties [13]. In recent years, numerous studies have been carried out using acidic DESs, such as Brønsted acidic DESs (BADESs) or Lewis acidic DESs (LADESs) for the fractionation and valorization of biomass [14]. In Lewis acidic DESs, these compounds with Lewis acidity are usually combined with other compounds (e.g., urea, ethylene glycol, etc.) to form eutectic mixtures through hydrogen bonding [15,16]. For example, the introduction of Lewis acids (AlCl3, FeCl3, FeCl2, ZnCl2 and CuCl2) into choline chloride/glycerol to make a ternary DES for the efficient pretreatment of hybrid beteljack energy grasses produces high purity and oxidative-resistant lignin [17]. In Brønsted acidic DESs, these acidic compounds usually combine with hydrogen bonding acceptors (e.g., quaternary ammonium salts, alcohols, etc.) to form eutectic mixtures with low melting points and high stability [18]. For example, DESs combined with choline chloride (ChCl) and natural p-coumaric acid (PCA) was applied for pretreatment on switchgrass under 160 °C, which induced 70 % of xylan removal [19]. However, acidic DESs will provide protons to catalyze the random cleavage of glycosidic bonds in xylan, leading to its hydrolysis to xylose, which was possibly dehydrated to furfural catalyzed by Brønsted and Lewis acids [20]. These degradation products will inhibit downstream hydrolysis and fermentation, which must be achieved after the detoxification process continued efficient biotransformation [21]. Therefore, in order to maximize product revenues from lignocellulosic, it is important to adopt efficient DESs to deal with the challenges of acidic conditions. Compared to neutral or acidic environments, polysaccharides showed less degradation under mild alkaline DESs conditions, which also effectively reduce the formation of inhibitors [22]. Meanwhile, the recovered hemicellulose has a higher molecular weight, thus adding additional high economic value to the production process [23]. It is also deserved to note that, lignin condensation also occurs in the intense acid treatment, hindering further bioconversion of the treated lignocellulose. Comparatively, alkali treatment process usually does not require high temperatures and also reduces the occurrence of condensation reactions [24,25]. For example, alkaline DESs (choline chloride/glycol/Na2S) incorporated by Na2S greatly facilitated the decomposition of lignin with a removal rate of up to 74.67%, while maximizing the retention of glucan and hemicellulose [26]. Thus, it is crucial and emerging to find suitable alkaline DESs to achieve efficient biotransformation. Among the chemicals consisting of alkaline DESs, choline hydroxide (ChOH) is an aqueous, low-cost, biodegradable basic ionic liquid, which can act as effictive HBA and provide an alkaline environment for DESs [27]. For example, choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) DESs with 11 wt % water were used to dissolve at least 9.5 wt% cellulose with the degree of polymerization (DP) of 926 within 30 min [10]. Pan and colleagues applied two choline hydroxide based DESs (choline hydroxide-glycerol and choline hydroxide-urea) pretreatment on wheat straw. It removed 73.9% and 75.6% of lignin respectively, which showed a better coupling effect than choline chloride acid DESs [28]. These literatures indicate that, ChOH-based DESs have great potential for pretreatment of biomass. Besides, natural origin of the components gives DESs a great edge over DESs because they are clearly less toxic and more environ- mentally friendly. Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESS) include amino acid-glycosyl DESs, amino acid-organic acid-DESs, and glycosyl DESs etc. [29-31]. Recently, our group reported a novel arginine/ lactic acid DES (1:7) pretreatment strategy on moso bamboo, reaching high lignin removal rate of 84.4% and the highest enzymatic conversion yield of 81.9% glucose [32]. Pretreatment on corncob by DESs con- sisting of amino acids (lysine, arginine, histidine) and betaine for 5 h at 60 °C, about 50% of xylan and 60% of lignin could be removed, as well as obtaining enzymatic hydrolysis yield of 60.8% [33]. These results demonstrated satisfactory lignin and hemicellulose extraction, along with a high hydrolysis rate, using NADESs pretreatments. The remarkable bioconversion performance makes NADESS well suited for the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. However, up till now, there are very limited reports on ChOH as a prerequisite for NADESS with the cooperation of bio-derived amino acid. Moreover, the attempt to apply ChOH-based NADESs on biomass treatment and the inner mechanisms on lignocellulose deconstruction have been rarely discussed. In this study, natural choline hydroxide/arginine (CA) DESs were developed for the first time to pretreat highly recalcitrant moso bamboo with the assistance of microwave radiation in short treatment time. The polarity and viscosity of DESs with different molar ratios were studied and their pretreatment properties were characterized. The effect of DESs on the cell wall structure of bamboo was described through scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and laser confocal technology. X-ray diffraction was used to study the variations of aggregated and crystalline cellulose under the treatment of DESs and characterization of extracted lignin by 2D HSQC NMR spectroscopy. The correlation between lignin removal, xylan removal, crystal size of cellulose, and enzymatic hy- drolysis yield was analyzed to explore the influencing factors of enzy- matic hydrolysis. The DESs pretreatment strategy of bamboo was evaluated by material balance accounting. The present study proposing physicochemical properties and pretreatment effects of DESs may pro- vide a reliable basis for further application of biorefinery on lignocel- lulosic biomass by alkaline NADESs. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and chemicals Moso bamboo culms were provided by Yunnan Forestry Center. Bamboo powder (40–80 mesh) was extracted by soxhlet extraction (acetone–ethanol volume ratio 2:1) for 6 h to remove pigments and alcohols. Bamboo strips were cut into 10 µm-sized transverse and radial sections using a slicer (HM 325, Thermo Scientific, USA) and observed under microscope. L-arginine and choline hydroxide were obtained from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All other chemicals were purchased from Shanghai Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China) and used as received. 2.2. DES preparation and characterization Choline hydroxide solution was slowly dripped into arginine solution at a molar ratio of 1:1/ 2:1 with homogeneous stirring for 24 h. The mixture was rotary evaporated under negative pressure at 50 °C to remove water and dried under vacuum at 70 °C for 48 h. The prepared DESs were left overnight to observe their stability. The DES with molar ratios of 1:1 and 1:2 (arginine to choline) are labeled as CA1 and CA2, respectively, as shown in Table S1. The α, β, and π* of the prepared DESs were determined using N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (NEt2), 4-nitroaniline (NH2), and Nile red (NR) as dye indicators of solvent properties [34]. The maximum absorption wavelength λmax of the dye-DES mixture was determined between 350–700 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer and measured three times to minimize experimental errors. The mixture was heated at 600 W for 10 min and kept for 5 min using MDS-8G microwave disin- tegrator (SINEO, Shanghai, China). The microwave temperatures were set to 90 °C, 100 °C, 110 °C, 120 °C and 130 °C, respectively. At the end of the reaction, the solid residue was washed with 50% acetone solution and 1% NaOH aqueous solution, and then the solid residue was washed repeatedly with deionized water for neutrality. Part of the neutral ma- terial will be air-dried for subsequent testing and part will be placed at 4 °C for cellulase hydrolysis. The pretreated samples were named ac- cording to the type of DES and the pretreatment temperature, e.g., CA1 bamboo chips pretreated at 90 °C supplemented with microwave were called CA1-90, and the other samples were followed similarly. DES characterization The viscosity and Kamlet-Taft lysochromic parameters of two different molar ratios of DESs were characterized, and the results are listed in Table 1. Viscosity is an important parameter for DESs as solvents. The viscosities of CA1 and CA2 viscosity at room temperature, are 1026.3 mPa·s and 983.6 mPa·s, respectively. The values were far lower than the other arginine DESs, and even lower than the water content of 6.5 % wt of choline chloride-lactic acid classic system [37,38]. The low viscosity is conducive to the contact between DESs and bamboo feedstock, which may deconstructs lignocellulose through macromolecular mobility in shorter time [39]. The chemical properties of the proposed DESs are reflected by Kamlet-Taft solvent chromism parameters, which include α (hydrogen-bond acidity), β (hydrogen-bond basicity), and π* (polarity/polariz-ability) values [35]. DES with a larger (β-α) (net alkalinity) value is beneficial for dissolving lignin, while the solubility of xylan is linearly related to the β value [40]. As inferred from Table 1, the π* parameters are 1.270 (CA1) and 1.284 (CA2) respectively, which shows their high polarity and ability to construct non-specific interactions such as dipo-le-dipole interactions [41]. Meanwhile, CA1 and CA2 exhibit high (β-α) values, indicating their superior lignin removal performance when treating moso bamboo [42]. Higher β values of choline-arginine-based DES suggest a stronger hydrogen bond donor capacity of the DES. Be-sides, DES with high (β-α) values can form stronger hydrogen bonds with lignin and xylan, facilitating breakage of their non-covalent linkages with cellulose. Therefore, DES with higher β values and (β-α) values are more effective in the pretreatment of moso bamboo biomass [41]. 3.2. The cellulose recovery of bamboo after CA1 pretreatment was generally above 90 %, but it decreased to 86.4 % after CA2 pretreatment. For example, acidic ChCl/ethylene glycol (EG) DESs were developed and with the optimizing of alkali dosage, the cellulose recovery decreased from 87.43 % to 79.91 % [44]. Enzymatic hydrolysis The enzymatic hydrolysis yield is considered as an important index to evaluate the pretreatment effect of DESs. As shown in Fig. 2, direct cellulase hydrolysis of the original sample for 72 h resulted in a rather low glucose yield of 6.2%, which is consistent with previous research [50] (Fig. 2a). After pretreatment by CA1 and CA2, the glucose yield of bamboo increased to 69.5%–91.8% and 72.0%–86.0% (Fig. 2b and c), respectively. The glucose yields were 11.2–14.8 and 11.6–13.9 times higher than those of the original samples, respectively. Microwave-assisted CA1 reaction at 130 °C for 15 min can increase the glucose yield to 91.8%, and CA2 reaction at 90 °C can increase the conversion rate to 86.0%. Its high β value (0.845) and (β-α) value (0.554) demonstrate high selectivity for delignification, excellent carbohydrate recovery, and desirable fermentable sugar yields. Under optimal conditions (130 °C, 15 min, arginine:ChOH = 1:1, 20 FPU/g), it achieved a high delignification rate (94.4%) and xylan removal rate (75.6%), resulting in enhanced dual monosaccharide yields, with 91.8 % glucose yield and 71.4% xylose yield. Moreover, in the alkaline environment, the degradation of polysaccharides was greatly minimized, and the cleavage of alkali-unstable FA and PCA by choline-arginine DESs was observed, which were considered favorable factors for improving enzymatic hydrolysis yields. Pretreatment conditions under selected microwave-assisted methods were more effective in both improving results and reducing energy consumption compared to conventional heating conditions. Overall, the proposed arginine/ChOH DESs pretreatment strategy proved to be a low-cost and effective method, showing great application potential for lignocellulose deconstruction and conversion into bio-based chemicals. Herein, novel alkaline arginine-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) pretreatment was employed to achieve efficient fractionation of highly recalcitrant moso bamboo. Higher solvent basicity was revealed for the proposed DESs with Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters values of α (0.292), β (0.845), and π* (1.284). Thus, a high (β-α) value was achieved, favorable for forming stronger hydrogen bonds with lignin and xylan for subsequent separation. Supramolecular structural changes of DESs-treated bamboo cellulose were quantitatively calculated, suggesting increased crystallinity index and decreased crystallite size that were beneficial for the following enzymatic degradation. The DESs pretreatment dramatically increased the removal rate of lignin (as high as 94.4%) and xylan (75.6%), greatly enhancing subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis with the highest saccharification yield rate of 91.8%, 9.8 folds as compared to that of raw bamboo biomass. Critical factors affecting enzymatic conversion performance of the bamboo cellulose were integrated, showing strong correlations with xylan removal (R² = 0.91), lignin removal (R² = 0.99), and cellulose crystallite size reduction (R² = 0.852). Introduction Due to overconsumption of fossil resources and serious environ- mental pollution, exploration for environmentally friendly and renew- able alternatives has received more and more attention [1]. In recent decades, biorefining of lignocellulosic biomass has been considered as an ideal approach [2,3]. However, the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic biomass, such as moso bamboo, induced by the factors of lignin content, cell wall thickness, cellulose crystallinity, polymer orientation, lignin- carbohydrate complex (LCC) linkages, hemicellulose branching, and intricate anatomical structures etc., has consistently posed a significant barrier to the efficient conversion of biomass into renewable energy and chemicals [4,5]. Therefore, exploring fascinating solvents for effective pretreatment and deconstruction of recalcitrant lignocellulose cell walls, as well as separating the major components for further bioconversion remain a hot topic but not well addressed. Among the reported lignocellulosic pretreatment approaches, ionic liquids (ILs) have emerged as promising solvents for biomass pretreat- ment due to their wide liquid range, high solvating ability, and high ionic conductivity [6]. While, growing environmental and economic concerns limit their industrial applications [7]. With the introduction and development of green chemistry, the adoption of low- environmental impact processing technologies for producing high- value-added products from lignocellulosic raw materials has become a * Corresponding author. Recently, DESs have stood out in green biocatalysis and biotransformation with the advantages of low cost, simple synthesis, and environmental sustainability. DESs are consist of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), usually using quaternary ammonium salts as HBAs, and acids, bases, carbohydrates, and phenolic substances as HBDs [11,12]. Therefore, DESs consisting different molar ratios of HBAs and HBDs may have many possible combinations, affecting their physical and chemical properties [13]. In recent years, numerous studies have been carried out using acidic DESs, such as Brønsted acidic DESs (BADESs) or Lewis acidic DESs (LADESs) for the fractionation and valorization of biomass [14]. In Lewis acidic DESs, these compounds with Lewis acidity are usually combined with other compounds (e.g., urea, ethylene glycol, etc.) to form eutectic mixtures through hydrogen bonding [15,16]. For example, the introduction of Lewis acids (AlCl3, FeCl3, FeCl2, ZnCl2 and CuCl2) into choline chloride/glycerol to make a ternary DES for the efficient pretreatment of hybrid beteljack energy grasses produces high purity and oxidative-resistant lignin [17]. In Brønsted acidic DESs, these acidic compounds usually combine with hydrogen bonding acceptors (e.g., quaternary ammonium salts, alcohols, etc.) to form eutectic mixtures with low melting points and high stability [18]. For example, DESs combined with choline chloride (ChCl) and natural p-coumaric acid (PCA) was applied for pretreatment on switchgrass under 160 °C, which induced 70 % of xylan removal [19]. However, acidic DESs will provide protons to catalyze the random cleavage of glycosidic bonds in xylan, leading to its hydrolysis to xylose, which was possibly dehydrated to furfural catalyzed by Brønsted and Lewis acids [20]. These degradation products will inhibit downstream hydrolysis and fermentation, which must be achieved after the detoxification process continued efficient biotransformation [21]. Therefore, in order to maximize product revenues from lignocellulosic, it is important to adopt efficient DESs to deal with the challenges of acidic conditions. Compared to neutral or acidic environments, polysaccharides showed less degradation under mild alkaline DESs conditions, which also effectively reduce the formation of inhibitors [22]. Meanwhile, the recovered hemicellulose has a higher molecular weight, thus adding additional high economic value to the production process [23]. It is also deserved to note that, lignin condensation also occurs in the intense acid treatment, hindering further bioconversion of the treated lignocellulose. Comparatively, alkali treatment process usually does not require high temperatures and also reduces the occurrence of condensation reactions [24,25]. For example, alkaline DESs (choline chloride/glycol/Na2S) incorporated by Na2S greatly facilitated the decomposition of lignin with a removal rate of up to 74.67%, while maximizing the retention of glucan and hemicellulose [26]. Thus, it is crucial and emerging to find suitable alkaline DESs to achieve efficient biotransformation. Among the chemicals consisting of alkaline DESs, choline hydroxide (ChOH) is an aqueous, low-cost, biodegradable basic ionic liquid, which can act as effictive HBA and provide an alkaline environment for DESs [27]. For example, choline hydroxide/urea (ChOH/Ur) DESs with 11 wt % water were used to dissolve at least 9.5 wt% cellulose with the degree of polymerization (DP) of 926 within 30 min [10]. Pan and colleagues applied two choline hydroxide based DESs (choline hydroxide-glycerol and choline hydroxide-urea) pretreatment on wheat straw. It removed 73.9% and 75.6% of lignin respectively, which showed a better coupling effect than choline chloride acid DESs [28]. These literatures indicate that, ChOH-based DESs have great potential for pretreatment of biomass. Besides, natural origin of the components gives DESs a great edge over DESs because they are clearly less toxic and more environ- mentally friendly. Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESS) include amino acid-glycosyl DESs, amino acid-organic acid-DESs, and glycosyl DESs etc. [29-31]. Recently, our group reported a novel arginine/ lactic acid DES (1:7) pretreatment strategy on moso bamboo, reaching high lignin removal rate of 84.4% and the highest enzymatic conversion yield of 81.9% glucose [32]. Pretreatment on corncob by DESs con- sisting of amino acids (lysine, arginine, histidine) and betaine for 5 h at 60 °C, about 50% of xylan and 60% of lignin could be removed, as well as obtaining enzymatic hydrolysis yield of 60.8% [33]. These results demonstrated satisfactory lignin and hemicellulose extraction, along with a high hydrolysis rate, using NADESs pretreatments. The remarkable bioconversion performance makes NADESS well suited for the pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass. However, up till now, there are very limited reports on ChOH as a prerequisite for NADESS with the cooperation of bio-derived amino acid. Moreover, the attempt to apply ChOH-based NADESs on biomass treatment and the inner mechanisms on lignocellulose deconstruction have been rarely discussed. In this study, natural choline hydroxide/arginine (CA) DESs were developed for the first time to pretreat highly recalcitrant moso bamboo with the assistance of microwave radiation in short treatment time. The polarity and viscosity of DESs with different molar ratios were studied and their pretreatment properties were characterized. The effect of DESs on the cell wall structure of bamboo was described through scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and laser confocal technology. X-ray diffraction was used to study the variations of aggregated and crystalline cellulose under the treatment of DESs and characterization of extracted lignin by 2D HSQC NMR spectroscopy. The correlation between lignin removal, xylan removal, crystal size of cellulose, and enzymatic hy- drolysis yield was analyzed to explore the influencing factors of enzy- matic hydrolysis. The DESs pretreatment strategy of bamboo was evaluated by material balance accounting. The present study proposing physicochemical properties and pretreatment effects of DESs may pro- vide a reliable basis for further application of biorefinery on lignocel- lulosic biomass by alkaline NADESs. ## 2. DES characterization The viscosity and Kamlet-Taft lysochromic parameters of two different molar ratios of DESs were characterized, and the results are listed in Table 1. Viscosity is an important parameter for DESs as solvents. The viscosities of CA1 and CA2 viscosity at room temperature, are 1026.3 mPa·s and 983.6 mPa·s, respectively. The values were far lower than the other arginine DESs, and even lower than the water content of 6.5 % wt of choline chloride-lactic acid classic system [37,38]. The low viscosity is conducive to the contact between DESs and bamboo feedstock, which may deconstructs lignocellulose through macromolecular mobility in shorter time [39]. The chemical properties of the proposed DESs are reflected by Kamlet-Taft solvent chromism parameters, which include α (hydrogen-bond acidity), β (hydrogen-bond basicity), and π* (polarity/polariz-ability) values [35]. DES with a larger (β-α) (net alkalinity) value is beneficial for dissolving lignin, while the solubility of xylan is linearly related to the β value [40]. As inferred from Table 1, the π* parameters are 1.270 (CA1) and 1.284 (CA2) respectively, which shows their high polarity and ability to construct non-specific interactions such as dipo-le-dipole interactions [41]. Meanwhile, CA1 and CA2 exhibit high (β-α) values, indicating their superior lignin removal performance when treating moso bamboo [42]. Higher β values of choline-arginine-based DES suggest a stronger hydrogen bond donor capacity of the DES. Be-sides, DES with high (β-α) values can form stronger hydrogen bonds with lignin and xylan, facilitating breakage of their non-covalent linkages with cellulose. Therefore, DES with higher β values and (β-α) values are more effective in the pretreatment of moso bamboo biomass [41]. 3.2. The cellulose recovery of bamboo after CA1 pretreatment was generally above 90 %, but it decreased to 86.4 % after CA2 pretreatment. For example, acidic ChCl/ethylene glycol (EG) DESs were developed and with the optimizing of alkali dosage, the cellulose recovery decreased from 87.43 % to 79.91 % [44]. Enzymatic hydrolysis The enzymatic hydrolysis yield is considered as an important index to evaluate the pretreatment effect of DESs. As shown in Fig. 2, direct cellulase hydrolysis of the original sample for 72 h resulted in a rather low glucose yield of 6.2%, which is consistent with previous research [50] (Fig. 2a). After pretreatment by CA1 and CA2, the glucose yield of bamboo increased to 69.5%–91.8% and 72.0%–86.0% (Fig. 2b and c), respectively. The glucose yields were 11.2–14.8 and 11.6–13.9 times higher than those of the original samples, respectively. It was higher than the conversion of samples pretreated with guanidine hydrochloride (GH)/urea (U) (90.79 wt%), GH/glycerol (Gly) (86.67 wt%), choline chloride/lactic acid (LA) (72.56 wt%), and GH/LA (50.09 wt%) DESs at 130 °C for 30 min [51]. The removal of lignin-carbohydrate complex by the DESs may be one of the major factors for improving the accessibility of enzymes to cellulose chains. Microwave-assisted CA1 reaction at 130 °C for 15 min can increase the glucose yield to 91.8%, and CA2 reaction at 90 °C can increase the conversion rate to 86.0%. The phenomena suggested the ideal pretreatment efficiency by choline-arginine DES properties. With respect to conversion of hemicelluloses, the yield of xylose increased from 8.9% to 56.8%–71.4% for CA1 and 8.9% to 68.0%–76.8% for CA2 (Fig. 2d, e and f). It has been reported that, alkaline DESs showed the capability to saponify and split the ester bonds between hemicellulose and other components [50]. In addition to the removal of acetyl groups and the weakening of hydrogen bonds between cellulose and hemicellulose, satisfying enzymatic degradability on both cellulose and hemicelluloses saccharides were achieved [54]. In order to furtherly show the relationship between the lignin and xylan removal rate by DESs and glucose yields by enzymatic hydrolysis, linear fitting plot was performed. However, CA2 removal rate was negatively correlated with glucose yield. This is related to the structural changes caused by the removal of the outer envelope structure of cellulose in a highly alkaline environment [55]. 3.4. Lignin characteristics 2D-HSQC NMR spectroscopy was used to investigate the chemical structural variations of lignin after DESs pretreatment. The two-dimensional map information of aliphatic region and aromatic region is shown in Fig. 7 and annotated according to previous literature [66]. Typical bonds of lignin were present in all samples, including β-O-4 bond structure (A), β-β bond structure (B), and β-5 bond structure (C). Moreover, The observation of γ-acetylated β-O-4 bond (A') signals in pristine lignin samples represents the acetylation of the γ-C site of lignin and the appearance of acylated p-coumaric acid structure [8]. However, the signal was weakened under CA2 treatment at 90 °C and disappeared after CA1 treatment at 130 °C, indicating that the acetyl group was shed under alkaline DESs pretreatment and eliminated at high temperature [67]. At the same time, Aα, Aβ (S), and Aβ (G) correspond to Cα-Hα, Cβ-Hβ in β-O-4 bond of eugenic-based lignin and Cβ-Hβ in β-O-4 bond of guaiac-based lignin, respectively. Conclusion This study developed a rapid microwave-assisted choline-arginine deep eutectic solvent (DES) pretreatment to optimize the fractionation and enzymatic conversion of moso bamboo lignocellulose, revealing its high potential for selective delignification, carbohydrate recovery, and fermentable sugar production. Its high β value (0.845) and (β-α) value (0.554) demonstrate high selectivity for delignification, excellent carbohydrate recovery, and desirable fermentable sugar yields. Under optimal conditions (130 °C, 15 min, arginine:ChOH = 1:1, 20 FPU/g), it achieved a high delignification rate (94.4%) and xylan removal rate (75.6%), resulting in enhanced dual monosaccharide yields, with 91.8 % glucose yield and 71.4% xylose yield. Moreover, in the alkaline environment, the degradation of polysaccharides was greatly minimized, and the cleavage of alkali-unstable FA and PCA by choline-arginine DESs was observed, which were considered favorable factors for improving enzymatic hydrolysis yields. Pretreatment conditions under selected microwave-assisted methods were more effective in both improving results and reducing energy consumption compared to conventional heating conditions. Overall, the proposed arginine/ChOH DESs pretreatment strategy proved to be a low-cost and effective method, showing great application potential for lignocellulose deconstruction and conversion into bio-based chemicals.
